subject: english-literature
title: Context and Comparison
welcome_lead: Even with an unseen poem, you bring context. And many exam tasks ask comparison. Master both moves.
meta_desc: Contextualising unseen poetry and comparative tasks at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You can now situate the unseen poem in tradition and pair it with another for confident comparison.

concepts.def: Even without biographical knowledge, lexis, form and reference can suggest period, place and ideology.
Recognising echoes of earlier forms (pastoral, sonnet, war poetry) frames interpretation.
Connecting two poems on a thematic axis using connective vocabulary (similarly, whereas).
Where two poems agree, and where they differ — both are arguable.
Same theme, opposite tones (war poem ironic vs heroic) produces fertile contrast.
A sonnet alongside free verse signals different reader contracts.

walkthroughs.body_html:
A poem about trenches, gas and barbed wire situates itself in the First World War without naming dates.

Always justify contextual claims with textual evidence.
For comparison, decide the axis. Same theme, different mode? Same form, different politics? Begin with the axis and let details follow.
Owen's Dulce et Decorum Est and Brooke's The Soldier share the war theme but oppose it tonally. The contrast becomes the essay.
